newsitem.title: GHANA: Ghana economy pays price for 1992 wrong turn.
newsitem.headline: Ghana economy pays price for 1992 wrong turn.

text.p: Ghana, once hailed by the World Bank as a model pupil, took a wrong turn in 1992 and its economy is still paying the price, the Bank and independent economists say.
Joe Abbey, head of the Centre for Policy Analysis, an independent think-tank, goes as far as to say that the West African gold and cocoa producing nation has lost its way.

Faint hope comes from signs of foreign investment starting to pick up, but there is widespread agreement that Ghana still has a long way to go before most of its 18 million people feel the benefits of a decade of painful economic belt-tightening.
"I know full well that you are in a very difficult stage now," World Bank President James Wolfensohn told Ghana's newly elected parliament on Tuesday.

"It is quite hard to have a strong macroeconomic plan when there are social demands and poverty is rife in the country. But a macroeconomic plan which is sound is really an essential prerequisite to development," he said.
World Bank officials say Ghana's problems date back to a decision to give its civil servants an 80 percent pay increase before the 1992 national elections.
"All in all, Ghana has done well up to 1992 and then some bad decisions were taken for which they are paying the price now," says World Bank resident representative Kaikhosrou Framji.
GHANA SUCCESS OVERSTATED?
The World Bank heralded Ghana's economic adjustment as a success and an example to other African countries at a time when it had few other examples to fall back on.

"Proclaiming Ghana to be a 'success story' may not be accurate nor in the country's best interest," the Bank's 1996 Ghana Country Assistance Review says. "This may have contributed to some slackening in Ghana's own efforts from around 1989."
President Jerry Rawlings avoided making the same pay-rise mistake before last December's elections, in which he won a second and final term and his party maintained a majority in parliament.
But the damage had already been done.

"It was just really one incident which triggered a whole string of unfortunate macroeconomic consequences," Framji says, noting that the government found itself forced to increase the money supply and public borrowing.
Poor harvests in 1993 and 1994 compounded the problem, sending prices rocketing.
"There was also excess public sector borrowing which had to be financed so money supply sort of shot up and got relatively out of control," Framji said.
Today, Ghana finds itself over-reliant on foreign aid and struggling to meet International Monetary Fund targets, set as part of its economic reform programme.
SO WHAT'S THE SOLUTION?
"What is needed today is a strategy that makes a break-through in the investment climate and business environment for the private sector," the World Bank review says.
It produced a long list of shortcomings.
"Ghana's agenda of unfinished adjustment is a long one and the prospects for sustaining a satisfactory rate of per capita growth and poverty alleviation are uncertain," it said.

"Performance has been disappointing in private sector development, privatisation and public enterprise restructuring, civil service reform, expenditure control, agricultural development, educational achievement, environmental control and institutional development," it continued. There was more.
Private savings and investment rates "remain extremely low".
On the plus side the report lists progress in getting prices right, in rehabilitating infrastructure, in rationalising the revenue structure, and in public investment programming.
SIGNS OF INVESTMENT GROWTH

The Ghana Investment Promotion Centre (GIPC) says in 1996 it registered direct non-mining foreign private sector investments totalling $193 million, against $150 million in 1995 -- and that was in an election year with all its attendant uncertainty.
In the early 1990s the annual figure averaged $21 million.
Figures for the booming mining sector, which grew 5.5 percent in 1995, were not immediately available.
On the down side, foreign aid is six percent of Gross Domestic Product and the government has had trouble controlling some key indicators.
Money supply rose 48 percent in the year to September 1996. Domestic and foreign debt and the budget deficit have risen.

Inflation fell from 70 percent to 35 percent in the year to December 1996. "Whether that is sustainable is the big issue," Framji says, attributing the fall to lower food prices following good rainfall in 1995 and 1996.
Joe Abbey, a member of the board of the central bank, the Bank of Ghana, says inflation and public spending are the main symptoms of Ghana's economic malaise.
"We are going to have to decide with what criteria to regain budgetary balance," he adds, saying government spending needs to be carefully targeted.
The aim, he said, was "macroeconomic stability, followed by a return of confidence in the economy, followed by direct foreign investments and domestic savings."

Ghana has averaged GDP growth of five percent a year over the past decade but the Bank says that with population growth of three percent a year the country will take until 2030 to reach the still-low per capita income of $900. -- Abidjan newsroom +225 21 90 90
